_comment: Body risks and monitoring for each real mission in missions.json. Risk levels (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH) are our own summary for the demo, but every 'why' is based on what NASA, ESA or the mission's published study reported (links in missions.json 'sources'). Not medical advice. Keys under body_risks match content.json body_parts; keys under monitoring match health_rules.json indicators.

crew13_iss.headline: Six months weightless: bones and muscles weaken, fluid shifts to the head, but Earth is only a call away.

skeleton.why: NASA: astronauts lose about 1–1.5% of bone density per month in microgravity, even with exercise.

muscles.why: Leg and back muscles shrink when they never hold you up; ISS crews exercise about 2 hours a day to slow it.

eyes.why: About 70% of long-stay ISS astronauts show signs of SANS: fluid pushed toward the head changes the eye and optic nerve.

heart.why: Blood shifts upward and the heart does less work, so blood pressure and heart shape change over months.

brain.why: 16 sunrises a day and a busy schedule disturb the body clock, sleep and focus.

immune.why: Stress, a sealed cabin and some radiation (80–160 mSv in 6 months) put the immune system on alert.

stomach.why: Regular cargo flights keep food varied; the main watch item is drinking enough, because thirst feels weaker in 0 g.

monitoring.why: The main defence against bone and muscle loss in 0 g.
Catches changes caused by fluid moving toward the head.
Shows if the heart is adapting or struggling.
16 sunrises a day confuse the body clock.
Early sign of stress from six months in a small crew.
Thirst feels weaker in 0 g, so crews drink too little.
Recycled cabin air: a low reading can flag an air-quality problem.

twin_study.headline: A year in space changed one twin's genes, eyes, arteries and thinking speed. Most came back to normal, a few did not.

immune.why: Twin Study: over 1,000 genes changed, many tied to DNA repair and the immune system; some T-cell changes stayed after landing.

eyes.why: Scott's retina thickened and folds formed in the layer behind it (SANS), from fluid shifting toward the head.

heart.why: His carotid artery wall thickened early in the flight and stayed thicker for the rest of the mission.

brain.why: Thinking speed and accuracy dropped after landing and stayed lower for up to six months.

skeleton.why: A year of 0 g means a year of bone loss; exercise slowed it but did not stop it.

muscles.why: Body mass fell 7% in flight; returning to gravity brought joint and muscle pain for days.

stomach.why: Gut bacteria changed a lot in flight but stayed diverse and returned to normal on Earth: rated low risk.

monitoring.why: The Twin Study saw thinking speed slow, so track it before it affects work.
Artery and fluid changes show up in blood pressure first.
Baseline for heart and artery changes over a long stay.
The immune system stayed on high alert; a fever is an early warning.
A full year of bone and muscle loss to fight.
Long missions wear down sleep, which drags down mood and focus.
Almost a year away from family and Earth.

artemis2.headline: Ten days in deep space: radiation is the big new risk, inside a capsule the size of a campervan.

immune.why: Beyond Earth's magnetic field, galactic cosmic rays reach the crew. NASA's AVATAR chips flew crew bone marrow to study this.

brain.why: NASA's ARCHeR study tracked sleep, stress and teamwork in a tiny cabin with a demanding schedule.

eyes.why: The crew had eye and brain health checks before and after, because fluid shifts start within days of launch.

heart.why: Launch, high-speed reentry and fluid shifts strain the heart; blood samples tracked cardiovascular health.

muscles.why: Ten days is too short for big muscle loss, but balance and movement were tested after splashdown.

skeleton.why: Bone loss builds over months, not days.

stomach.why: Packed food for a short trip; the risk is space motion sickness in the first days.

monitoring.why: ARCHeR wristbands tracked sleep: tired crews make mistakes far from home.
Stress in a small capsule affects the whole team.
Deep-space radiation and fatigue can slow thinking before you notice.
Watches the heart through launch, flyby and reentry.
Early warning if radiation or stress weakens the immune system.
Orion's life support flew with people for the first time: check the air is doing its job.

mars520.headline: No radiation, no weightlessness, just 520 days sealed in: the crew slowed down, slept more and drifted off their body clocks.

brain.why: PNAS 2013: crews got more sedentary every month; one member drifted onto a 25-hour day, and 4 of 6 had issues that could be serious on a real trip.

muscles.why: Crews moved less and less while awake ('hypokinesis'), so muscles were used less over time.

immune.why: Mars-520 studies found heightened immune responses and changes in white blood cells during isolation.

heart.why: Normal gravity, but low activity over months is still bad for the heart.

skeleton.why: Full Earth gravity, so no space-style bone loss.

eyes.why: No weightlessness, so no fluid shift toward the head.

stomach.why: The crew ate an ISS-like diet; food got monotonous but was nutritionally fine.

monitoring.why: Sleep timing drifted badly: keep everyone on the same clock.
Fights the slow slide into doing less and less.
Monotony and isolation build up over many months.
Mars-520 tested crews weekly to spot tired or vulnerable members.
With a 20-minute delay to doctors, catch infections early.
Low activity shows up as a changing resting heart rate.

spacewalk.headline: Six to eight hours of hard work in vacuum inside a stiff suit: hands, shoulders and body heat take the hit.

muscles.why: NASA EVA report: hand, wrist and shoulder injuries are common; about 0.26 injuries were reported per spacewalk in one review.

heart.why: Hours of effort against a pressurised suit raise heart rate and body heat; Gemini 9's Cernan lost 13 lb of sweat.

immune.why: Only the suit shields you from radiation, so you get less protection than inside the station.

brain.why: Long, tiring tasks with no room for error; poor suit airflow can build up CO2 and cloud thinking.

skeleton.why: Decompression sickness can hit joints, so crews pre-breathe pure oxygen to flush out nitrogen first.

stomach.why: Only a small drink bag in the suit, and heavy sweating dehydrates you fast.

eyes.why: The visor protects the eyes; water leaking into the helmet (ISS EVA 23, 2013) is the rare but serious exception.

monitoring.why: Catches overexertion before it becomes dangerous.
Confirms the oxygen pre-breathe worked and nothing went wrong in the suit.
Heavy sweating in the suit; drink before and rehydrate after.
Overheating inside the suit is a real risk.
A tired spacewalker is a safety risk to the whole crew.
Hard work and pressure changes both move blood pressure.
